README: Conformance fixture from Particle-Academy/prism-parity. Verdicts in `expect_valid` and `expect_keyword` were produced by Python jsonschema 4.26.0 (Draft 2020-12), NOT by any JS implementation -- assert against these, not against your own output. Source of truth for the schema and documents is prism-parity main at c340b57.

id.description: Stable forever. NEVER renumbered — ids appear in other repos' skip lists and in probes/probes.json. Ids are unique and sorted ascending, which means a new case goes at the END of the file. File order is not chronology.

notes.description: REQUIRED. What this case exists to catch. A case without a stated purpose gets deleted by someone later who cannot tell it apart from its neighbour.

response.description: For kind=response-parse: the raw provider response body, exactly as the provider would send it.

subject.description: For kind=roundtrip: the value object under test.

skip.description: A MAP KEYED BY LANGUAGE. Never a scalar — a loader that reads this as truthy skips the row in every language at once AND makes the empty-reason guard unreachable, because a non-empty object is never blank. Both effects are silent. Every loader pins this from both directions.

additionalProperties.description: MANDATORY and non-empty, enforced at LOAD time in every loader. A skip that does not say why becomes permanent silently.

since.description: The corpus version this case was added in. Makes the age of a row visible without archaeology, and makes 'this went red after we upgraded' answerable.

tolerance.description: OPT-IN, PER-ROW, and visible in the row it applies to. Absent means EXACT comparison, which is the default and covers every case in the corpus today. A global epsilon is invisible — nobody reading a fixture can tell whether it asserts a value or a neighbourhood — and an invisible one lets two implementations that computed different values pass as equal, in the repository whose product is catching exactly that. When present, the comparison falls back to structural comparison with this absolute tolerance on numeric leaves. Do not add one without testing the justification first: see docs/decisions/0005-canonical-json.md.

left_raw.description: For kind=container-identity: one side of the pair, as RAW JSON TEXT. Text, not a decoded structure, because a decoded structure authored by running PHP cannot carry an array-versus-object distinction — PHP decodes {} and [] to the identical value. The raw string is the only channel that can hold what the reference language cannot express.

right_raw.description: For kind=container-identity: the other side of the pair, as RAW JSON TEXT.

body_json.description: Canonical JSON serialization of the provider request body. GENERATED by executing the reference implementation — never hand-authored. See docs/decisions/0005-canonical-json.md.

result_json.description: Canonical JSON serialization of the parsed result's array form. Generated by executing the reference implementation.

serialized_json.description: Canonical JSON serialization of the value object's stored form. Generated by executing the reference implementation.

rehydrates.description: When true the runner must also rebuild the value object from serialized_json and re-serialize it to the identical string.

error_code.description: A CODE, never a message. Error prose is worded idiomatically per language; pinning it holds every implementation to a translation and goes red on a wording improvement that changed nothing. The human sentence is explicitly outside the contract.

equal_after_parse.description: For kind=container-identity: whether the implementation's own JSON parser considers the two raw strings equal. A row of this kind has NO decoded input to fall back on, so it can only be answered by reading the raw strings — which is what proves the channel is wired to something rather than merely present.

builderScript.description: An ordered list of calls against the pending-request builder. Method names are the canonical (PHP) spelling; each language's runner maps them to its own idiom — with_prompt in Python, withPrompt in TypeScript. The contract is the call sequence, not the spelling.

construct.description: A tagged value-object constructor. '$' names the class; the remaining keys are constructor arguments by canonical name. Nested constructs are resolved depth-first.

guarded.description: Absent or true uses the guarded fetch; false exercises an existing unguarded path.

redirects_to.description: The Location returned by the fake HTTP response; normally the destination serves content.

redirects_always.description: When true, every fake response redirects to redirects_to, including requests already at that destination.

document.generated_by: tools/generate-agent-task-claim.php
document.scope: The claim and release state machine of an agent task list, and the canonical record it stores. NOT the completion tool, NOT the lease-extension path, and NOT the store's locking primitive -- each of those is a separate value with a separate failure mode, and this suite existing does not cover them.
document.recorded: Every row records the OUTCOME (ok or refused), the error CODE when refused, the canonical JSON of the affected record, and pending() afterwards. Codes rather than prose, per 0004: error messages are explicitly outside the contract.

cases.title: an ordinary claim from a two-task list
cases.notes: The control. If this row disagrees the claim path is wrong at the top and every row below it is noise.

cases.title: claim returns INSERTION order, never sorted
cases.notes: Ordering is the divergence class 0002 calls hardest to notice: nothing errors, the agent simply does the work in a different sequence and produces a different result. The ids are chosen so that alphabetical and insertion order DISAGREE.

cases.title: a claim against an empty list
cases.notes: Null, not an error. An empty list is a finished list, and that is how the loop terminates.

cases.title: every task claimed and none expired
cases.notes: Null again, for a different reason than atc-0003: there is work, it is simply not available.

cases.title: a lapsed lease returns the task to todo and NEVER to failed
cases.notes: A worker dying is not the task failing. Marking it failed burns a retry that never ran and tells the application something untrue about the work.

cases.title: expiry is INCLUSIVE: a lease is over AT its expiry
cases.notes: claimed_until equals now. A one-tick boundary difference between ports is a real divergence and nothing errors on it.

cases.title: release by the holder
cases.notes: The positive control for every refusal below it. Without this row they all pass on an implementation that refuses everything.

cases.title: release by someone who is NOT the holder
cases.notes: The sequence needs no adversary. Worker A's lease lapses, B reclaims and starts, A finishes late and overwrites B's live claim -- and B's own release then fails as already-terminal, so the second worker is blamed for the first one's mistake.

cases.title: release of a task nobody holds
cases.notes: Silence is not permission. Reading an unknowable holder as a match is the absent-outcome mistake asked about a different field.

cases.title: releasing a terminal task again
cases.notes: Terminal means terminal. A silent no-op here is how a second worker's result gets discarded with nothing saying so.

cases.title: an outcome the agent supplies is never coerced
cases.notes: The string complete is not done. Coercing anything-not-failed toward the PRIVILEGED outcome is an agent declaring victory by typo.

cases.title: an outcome padded with U+00A0 is not trimmed into validity
cases.notes: PHP's trim leaves U+00A0 and Python's strip takes it, so the same input has two answers unless the comparison is exact. That is the G-36 lesson asked about a different field.

cases.title: a worker id is compared exactly, with no trimming
cases.notes: A worker id padded with a trailing space is a DIFFERENT worker. Trimming would let one worker release another's task, and each language strips a different codepoint set.

cases.title: a blank worker id is refused
cases.notes: The empty string is falsy in PHP, so a blank owner would read as unclaimed. It has to be refused at the door rather than compared.

cases.title: a list ALREADY CONTAINING a duplicate id is read, not refused
cases.notes: Written expecting a refusal, and the reference does not refuse -- which is the finding. duplicate_task_id guards add(), the door this package controls. A list that already holds two tasks with one id is read back and counted. That matters precisely because the list is SHARED SURFACE: a port whose add() is less careful, or a hand-edited row, produces a list this one accepts, and find() then resolves the id to whichever comes first. Recorded as the behaviour rather than corrected to the expectation, because the expectation was mine and the behaviour is the contract's.

cases.title: a lease of zero is refused, not clamped
cases.notes: Accepting it silently is worse than clamping: claimed_until lands in the past, so the claim expires the instant it is granted and the next caller steals it. A lock that grants and immediately releases is indistinguishable from no lock.

cases.title: a FRACTIONAL lease is refused, not truncated
cases.notes: 90.4 becoming 90 is a configuration silently becoming a different configuration, which is the same rule as zero one scale down. claimed_until is an integer in all three languages, so it could never have been honoured as written.

skip.php: PHP cannot express this row: claim() declares ?int, so the value is rejected by the type system before any guard in the package runs. The reachable path in PHP is the configuration route, which is a different value and belongs in its own row.

cases.title: pending counts todo AND expired-claimed, and writes nothing
cases.notes: An expired claim is claimable, so it is pending. Counting it as held would stall a loop that still has work to do.

cases.title: find on an id that is not there
cases.notes: Null, not an error, and emphatically not the first task.

cases.title: the canonical record of an UNCLAIMED task
cases.notes: claimed_by and claimed_until must be PRESENT AND NULL, never absent. A port modelling unset as undefined drops the keys entirely and changes the bytes.

cases.title: claimed_until is an INTEGER timestamp, not a float or a date string
cases.notes: A float passes every equality assertion, because 1735689900.0 equals 1735689900, and renders differently in each language. Date FORMATTING is where three languages produce three strings from one instant.

cases.title: a completed message with no thinking reported
cases.notes: The baseline, and the CONTROL for every row below it. Anthropic sends no `output_tokens_details` at all when the model did not reason, so `thought_tokens` must come back null rather than zero: null means NOT MEASURED and zero means measured-as-none, and a caller tuning `effort` needs to tell those apart. Also pins that Anthropic reports cache tokens SEPARATELY from input_tokens rather than nested inside them, so nothing is subtracted from the prompt count the way the OpenAI mapping subtracts.

cases.title: thinking tokens reported, as a breakdown of the output count
cases.notes: The row G-48 existed for. Anthropic puts reasoning at usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens and EVERY language dropped it -- PHP omitted the argument, TypeScript passed a literal null, Python hardcoded None. Because all three agreed, no cross-language comparison could see it; it took a human measuring the live API (Moic Suite, prism#33). The numbers are the ones they measured on claude-opus-5 at effort:high, and they are chosen to be checkable: 1240 thinking INSIDE 2820 output. A consumer pricing completion + thought double-counts the expensive half, so the relationship is part of what this row pins, not just the field's presence.

cases.title: thinking tokens reported as ZERO
cases.notes: The row that would have caught the bug the fix nearly shipped. Python's first carry-forward used `or`, which treats 0 as absent -- so a model that reported zero thinking tokens would have silently inherited the previous count instead of reporting the zero. PHP and TypeScript use null-coalescing, which keeps it. Nothing in the corpus asserted a zero on this path, so the three languages could disagree here and stay green; it was caught by chance when ruff complained about line length. Zero and null must NOT collapse into each other: this row and atr-0001 differ only in that distinction.

cases.notes: Both breakdowns at once, because they are read from different places and one masking the other is exactly the kind of defect a single-field row cannot show. cases.title: a max_tokens finish still reports its usage
cases.notes: A non-`end_turn` finish, and the row that closed G-50. Anthropic signals a truncated turn with stop_reason `max_tokens`, and a turn that reasoned and then ran out of room is precisely when a caller most wants the thinking count -- it is the expensive case and the one that produced no useful answer. Both ports RAISED here until 2026-09-06 while the reference returned, so a caller got the text and usage in PHP and an exception in the other two. The ports now return, matching the reference. Note the reference is per-PROVIDER rather than uniform: Anthropic and Mistral return, OpenAI's Responses handler and its structured handler throw, and Azure throws -- so the ports were right about OpenAI all along, which is why seventeen OpenAI rows never surfaced this. It needed a max_tokens row, and there was none.

cases.title: two thinking blocks keep the FIRST block, not both joined
cases.notes: G-57. A signature covers exactly one block's text, so the text stored beside it has to be that block's. Both ports joined every thinking block's text until 2026-09-14; paired with one signature, joined text is a block Anthropic would refuse on replay. Keeping only the first loses the second block; whether Anthropic accepts a replay of one of two blocks has not been verified, and that question is open in G-57 for all three languages.

A language that failed the whole read on one malformed row would let a surface hide every change by including one bad one.

cases.title: nothing changed, and the surface was in a position to say so
cases.notes: One half of the pair that is the entire point of this suite.

cases.title: NOTHING CHANGED and CANNOT SAY are the same empty list on the wire
cases.notes: The other half, and the property this whole family exists for. Byte for byte the input is hpc-0009 without a marker; the answer must differ, because `answered` is false and `nothing_changed` must NOT be true. An agent that reads an unanswerable feed as quiet is the agent that reverts a person's edit believing it is fixing drift. A language that returned a bare list would agree with the others on the list and be dangerous in production.

cases.title: a surface admitting its answer is PARTIAL is not a surface reporting calm
cases.notes: The first surface asked hard-deletes rows with no tombstone, so a removal moves no revision and appears in no feed: `nothing changed` is what it says when a screen was destroyed. A package cannot detect that from outside — it can carry the admission, and `nothing_changed` must be false despite an empty list.

cases.title: `partial: true` is read as the inverse of complete
cases.notes: Two spellings of one fact, and a language reading only `complete` would report this answer as whole. The inversion is checked AFTER the positive key, so a surface sending both is read by the one it stated directly.

cases.title: a feed that has only ever said `agent` has proven nothing
cases.notes: Evidence when it arrives, never a precondition — the rule `ConflictDetection::Enforced` already follows. Naming the agent does not show a surface can tell a PERSON's edit from the agent's own, so the feed stays `offered`. The change is still not deferred to, because the surface positively said whose it was.

cases.title: a named hand other than the agent's upgrades the feed, and only the agent's own is excluded
cases.notes: The whole deference rule in one row. `defer_to` keeps the human's change and the unattributed one and drops only the change the surface said was the agent's. An earlier draft branched on whether the feed had PROVEN attribution and deferred to everything until it had, discarding per-change answers already given — not having information is a different mistake from throwing it away.

cases.title: attribution cannot upgrade a feed that cannot answer
cases.notes: A surface with no feed tool that somehow returns attributed rows has still not got a feed. Upgrading here would let a single crafted result make an unanswerable surface look `attributed` for the rest of the session, which is a state this package treats as permanent proof.

cases.title: `_meta` wins over the top level, the same order a revision is read in
cases.notes: MCP puts implementation data in `_meta`, so it is read first. A surface sending both is not a surface a package should have an opinion about — but the two languages that picked different ones would hand two agents different conversations.

cases.title: the top level is read when `_meta` has nothing to say
cases.notes: The fallback, pinned so it cannot quietly stop working. A surface with no `_meta` at all is the common shape outside MCP.

cases.title: spellings are matched case-insensitively and trimmed
cases.notes: Surfaces are written by people. Matching only the exact lowercase token would make this row `unknown`/`unknown` and silently stop deferring to a person's edit — the failure mode being guarded against, reached through capitalisation.

cases.title: a `changes` value that is not a list yields no rows rather than a crash
cases.notes: A hostile or broken surface sending an object where a list belongs must not take the turn down, and must not be read as one change either. The answer is an empty list from a feed that answered — which is exactly why `complete` and `answered` are separate from the list itself.

cases.title: handles are de-duplicated and keep first-seen order
cases.notes: An agent re-reads by handle, so the list it re-reads from must not contain the same handle twice or arrive in an order that differs by language. Insertion order, not sorted: sorting would be this package inventing a priority the surface did not state.

cases.title: an integral float revision, which is the G-35 shape in a new family
cases.notes: `human-plus-tool-admission` G-35 records that an integral float digests as `1` in PHP and JavaScript and `1.0` in Python. A revision marker is compared as text and echoed back on every later call, so the same split here would mean two agents pinning the same surface state to two different strings — and a surface enforcing the pin would refuse one of them. Carried as raw text so the float survives into the test.

cases.title: a FRACTIONAL revision is refused, because three languages cannot spell it alike
cases.notes: The boundary the hpc-0021 fix creates, and the reason it stops where it does. A whole number is accepted however the host decoded it; a fractional one is refused in all three. Not because a surface may not mint `1.5` — markers are opaque — but because a marker that is not byte-identical in every language is worse than no marker: it is echoed back on the next call, and a surface enforcing the pin would refuse whichever agent spelled it differently. Refusing loudly in three languages beats agreeing in two.

cases.title: a revision beyond safe-integer range is refused rather than rounded
cases.notes: The other end of the same boundary. Past 2^53-1 the three languages stop agreeing on what the number even is — JavaScript has no integer wider than a double, PHP casts to a platform int, Python does not — so a counter that grew that large would be pinned to three different strings. Refused everywhere, at the same threshold, spelled as a literal in all three rather than as each language's own MAX.

The two sides decode to the IDENTICAL value in PHP — verified, not assumed: json_decode('{}', true) === json_decode('[]', true) returns true — so the reference cannot answer it and is skipped. What makes it a probe is that it has no decoded input at all: a runner can only answer by parsing left_raw and right_raw itself. Presence of a raw-string field is trivially satisfied by the capture code and proves nothing; a row that can ONLY pass if the field was read is what proves the channel is wired to something. Without this row the entire raw-string mechanism could be inert and every test here would still be green. JSON APIs distinguish these constantly — empty tool lists, empty content arrays, empty metadata objects — so the distinction is not academic.

cases.title: a single component

cases.notes: The classic. 0.1 has no exact double, so this row pins that all three languages store the SAME inexact value rather than each rounding its own way. A language that parsed the literal differently would diverge here and nowhere else.

cases.title: full double precision
cases.notes: Seventeen significant digits. A format that round-tripped through a decimal string would lose the last one; this pins that it does not.

cases.title: alternating sign
cases.notes: Pins the sign bit across an even number of components, where a byte-order error inside a pair can cancel out and hide.

cases.title: both ends of the exponent range
cases.notes: Near the limits of a double. A format that narrowed to float32 anywhere in the path would overflow the second component to infinity and underflow the first to zero, and both would still base64 cleanly.

cases.title: eight components
cases.notes: Long enough that a chunking bug in the encoder has somewhere to show. Base64 encodes three bytes to four characters, so 64 bytes is not a multiple of the group size and the padding is exercised.

cases.title: no components at all
cases.notes: REFUSED in all three. An empty vector has no direction; storing one would put a row in the index that can never be scored and never be found.

cases.title: zero magnitude
cases.notes: REFUSED in all three, and the interesting one: it is not empty and every component is finite and valid. Its magnitude is zero, so similarity against it is undefined — and returning 0.0 would be a plausible-looking number rather than an answer.
